claim: Thermovibrio ammonificans is part of the phylum Aquificae, a deep-branching group of thermophilic bacteria found in geothermal environments.
source: Thermovibrio ammonificans is part of the phylum Aquificae, a deep-branching group of thermophilic bacteria found in geothermal environments (Lebedinsky et al., 2007; Sievert and Vetriani, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lebedinsky et al., 2007 and Sievert and Vetriani, 2012

claim: Based on phylogenetic analyses of the 16S rRNA gene as well as whole genomes, Aquificae are believed to be the earliest bacterial lineages having emerged on Earth along with the phyla Thermotogae and Thermodesulfobacteria.
source: Based on phylogenetic analyses of the 16S rRNA gene as well as whole genomes, Aquificae are believed to be the earliest bacterial lineages having emerged on Earth along with the phyla Thermotogae and Thermodesulfobacteria (Di Giulio, 2003; Pitulle et al., 1994; Battistuzzi et al., 2004) (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Giulio, 2003; Pitulle et al., 1994; Battistuzzi et al., 2004 and reference to Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: All the cultured members of the Aquificae phylum are chemolithoautotrophs that use hydrogen as an energy source.
source: All the cultured members of this phylum are chemolithoautotrophs that use hydrogen as an energy source, have optimum growth temperatures between 65˚C and 95°C and rely on the reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle (rTCA) to convert carbon dioxide into biomass (Hügler et al., 2007; Hügler and Sievert, 2011; Sievert and Vetriani, 2012) (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hügler et al., 2007; Hügler and Sievert, 2011; Sievert and Vetriani, 2012 and reference to Table 1

claim: All cultured members of the Aquificae phylum have optimum growth temperatures between 65˚C and 95°C.
source: All the cultured members of this phylum are chemolithoautotrophs that use hydrogen as an energy source, have optimum growth temperatures between 65˚C and 95°C and rely on the reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle (rTCA) to convert carbon dioxide into biomass (Hügler et al., 2007; Hügler and Sievert, 2011; Sievert and Vetriani, 2012) (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hügler et al., 2007; Hügler and Sievert, 2011; Sievert and Vetriani, 2012 and reference to Table 1

claim: All cultured members of the Aquificae phylum rely on the reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle (rTCA) to convert carbon dioxide into biomass.
source: All the cultured members of this phylum are chemolithoautotrophs that use hydrogen as an energy source, have optimum growth temperatures between 65˚C and 95°C and rely on the reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle (rTCA) to convert carbon dioxide into biomass (Hügler et al., 2007; Hügler and Sievert, 2011; Sievert and Vetriani, 2012) (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hügler et al., 2007; Hügler and Sievert, 2011; Sievert and Vetriani, 2012 and reference to Table 1

claim: The genome of T. ammonificans HB-1 consists of one chromosome and one plasmid of 1,682,965 bp and 76,561 bp, respectively.
source: The genome of T. ammonificans HB-1 consists of one chromosome and one plasmid of 1,682,965 bp and 76,561 bp, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2 showing genome structure

claim: The genome of T. ammonificans encodes for 1890 genes, 1831 of which are protein coding genes.
source: The genome encodes for 1890 genes, 1831 of which are protein coding genes and 75.16% of the protein coding genes could be assigned a putative function (Giovannelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giovannelli et al., 2012

claim: 75.16% of the protein coding genes in T. ammonificans could be assigned a putative function.
source: The genome encodes for 1890 genes, 1831 of which are protein coding genes and 75.16% of the protein coding genes could be assigned a putative function (Giovannelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giovannelli et al., 2012

claim: 780 proteins, comprising approximately 43% of all predicted ORFs in the database, were identified in cell samples of T. ammonificans grown under nitrate reducing conditions.
source: 780 proteins, comprising approximately 43% of all predicted ORFs in the database, were identified in cell samples of T. ammonificans grown under nitrate reducing conditions (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1 showing proteomic data

claim: The four key enzymes of the rTCA cycle together yielded a relative abundance of 6% of all identified proteins in T. ammonificans samples.
source: The four key enzymes of the rTCA cycle (see next paragraph for details) together yielded a relative abundance of 6% of all identified proteins in the samples.
evidence: Based on proteomic analysis data

claim: Most of the enzymes putatively involved in the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway in T. ammonificans, including the carbon-monoxide dehydrogenase (CodH), were detected in the proteome at a lower abundance of 1.25% of all proteins.
source: Most of the enzymes putatively involved in the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway (Table 2), including the carbon-monoxide dehydrogenase (CodH), were also detected, although at a lower abundance of 1.25% of all proteins.
evidence: Supported by reference to Table 2 and proteomic data

claim: The rTCA cycle is widespread among anaerobic and microaerophilic bacteria including all Aquificae, chemolithoautotrophic Epsilonproteobacteria, Chlorobi, and Nitrospirae.
source: The rTCA cycle is widespread among anaerobic and microaerophilic bacteria including all Aquificae, chemolithoautotrophic Epsilonproteobacteria, Chlorobi, and Nitrospirae (Berg, 2011; Fuchs, 2011; Hügler and Sievert, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Berg, 2011; Fuchs, 2011; Hügler and Sievert, 2011

claim: The reductive acetyl-CoA pathway is believed to be the most ancient carbon fixation pathway on Earth.
source: The reductive acetyl-CoA pathway is believed to be the most ancient carbon fixation pathway on Earth (Fuchs, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuchs, 2011

claim: T. ammonificans codes for the type V CodH, which is present in numerous deep-branching organisms.
source: However, rather than coding for the classical bifunctional type II CodH, T. ammonificans codes for the type V, which is present in numerous deep-branching organisms (Figure 4) and whose function is unknown (Techtmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Techtmann et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 4

claim: The function of type V CodH is unknown.
source: However, rather than coding for the classical bifunctional type II CodH, T. ammonificans codes for the type V, which is present in numerous deep-branching organisms (Figure 4) and whose function is unknown (Techtmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Techtmann et al., 2012

claim: The type V CodH may represent the most ancestral version of this class of enzymes based on structural and size considerations.
source: We hypothesize that the type V CodH, which, based on structural and size considerations may represent the most ancestral version of this class of enzymes (Frank Robb, personal communication), may catalyze the reduction of CO2 to CO.
evidence: Based on inference from structural and size considerations, supported by personal communication

claim: The codh gene of T. ammonificans shared high similarity (87%) with that of D. thermolithotrophum.
source: The codh gene of T. ammonificans shared high similarity with that of D. thermolithotrophum (87 similarity), while the similarity with the next closest homologous genes dropped below 54%.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: The genome of D. thermolithotrophum codes for a classical bifunctional Type II CodH in addition to the type V CodH.
source: The genome of D. thermolithotrophum also codes for a classical bifunctional Type II CodH (Dester_0417 and Dester_0418; Figure 4) in addition to the type V CodH.
evidence: Based on genome analysis and reference to Figure 4

claim: T. ammonificans uses the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway to synthesize pentose and hexose monosaccharides.
source: T. ammonificans uses the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway to synthesize pentose and hexose monosaccharides.
evidence: Based on genome analysis identifying key genes

claim: The fbp gene is present in Desulfurobacterium thermolithotrophum, Sulfurohydrogenibium sp. YO3AOP1, Persephonella marina and Hydrogenivirga sp. 128–5 R1-6, but absent from the genome of A. aeolicus and H. thermophilus.
source: While the fbp gene is present in Desulfurobacterium thermolithotrophum, and in the genome of Sulfurohydrogenibium sp. YO3AOP1, Persephonella marina and Hydrogenivirga sp. 128–5 R1-6, it is absent from the genome of A. aeolicus (Deckert et al., 1998) and H. thermophilus
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis and citation to Deckert et al., 1998

claim: Hydrogen is the only electron donor used by T. ammonificans.
source: Hydrogen is the only electron donor used by T. ammonificans and its importance in the metabolism of this bacterium is reflected by the diversity of hydrogenases found in the genome
evidence: Based on physiological characterization and genome analysis

claim: The Group 1 cluster in T. ammonificans (Hyn) is more similar to the hydrogenases found in Deltaproteobacteria than to homologs in other Aquificae.
source: Comparative analyses of the hydrogenases revealed that the Group 1 cluster in T. ammonificans (Hyn) is more similar to the hydrogenases found in Deltaproteobacteria than to homologs in other Aquificae (Figure 5).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: An event of lateral gene transfer occurred between T. ammonificans and the Deltaproteobacteria involving hydrogen oxidation Group 1 enzymes.
source: This finding raises interesting questions about the origin of the hydrogen oxidation Group 1 enzymes in T. ammonificans and suggests that an event of lateral gene transfer occurred between T. ammonificans and the Deltaproteobacteria.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis showing closer similarity to Deltaproteobacteria than to other Aquificae

claim: The periplasmic nitrate reductase (napA) and the nap operon structure in T. ammonificans appears to be closely related to that of Deltaproteobacteria.
source: Further, the periplasmic nitrate reductase (napA) and the nap operon structure in T. ammonificans also appears to be closely related to that of Deltaproteobacteria, suggesting that a horizontal gene transfer event involved the entire hydrogen oxidation (Hyn)/nitrate reduction respiratory pathway (see discussion).
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: T. ammonificans and D. thermolithotrophum genomes code for both Group 3 cytoplasmic hydrogenases, Group 3a F420-reducing hydrogenases (frhACB) and Group 3b multimeric cytoplasmic sulfhydrogenases (hydABCD).
source: Contrarily to members of the Aquificaceae and Hydrogenothermaceae, T. ammonificans and D. thermolithotrophum genomes code for both Group 3 cytoplasmic hydrogenases, Group 3a F420-reducing hydrogenases (frhACB) and Group 3b multimeric cytoplasmic sulfhydrogenases (hydABCD; Figure 5; Jeon et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on genome analysis and citation to Jeon et al., 2015, with reference to Figure 5

claim: Group 3 cytoplasmic hydrogenases have a polyphyletic origin.
source: Overall, these results imply a polyphyletic origin for the group 3 cytoplasmic hydrogenases.
evidence: Inferred from comparative phylogenetic analyses

claim: Group 2 hydrogenases are found in microaerobic members of the Aquificaceae and Hydrogenothermaceae and in microaerobic Epsiloproteobacteria but are not found in anaerobes.
source: Interestingly, Group 2 hydrogenases are found in microaerobic members of the Aquificaceae and Hydrogenothermaceae and in microaerobic Epsiloproteobacteria but are not found in anaerobes, suggesting a possible link with oxygen adaptation.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis across different organisms

claim: Group 3a hydrogenases are found in strict anaerobes, including T. ammonificans and methanogens.
source: In contrast, Group 3a is found in strict anaerobes, including T. ammonificans and methanogens (Figure 5).
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: T. ammonificans HB-1 can use nitrate as a terminal electron acceptor and reduces it to ammonium.
source: T. ammonificans HB-1 can use nitrate as a terminal electron acceptor and reduces it to ammonium (Vetriani et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vetriani et al., 2004

claim: The nap operon structure of T. ammonificans is unique to this organism and shares similarity with Desulfovibrio desulfuricans and other Deltaproteobacteria.
source: Comparative genomic analyses with genomes from Aquificae and Proteobacteria indicate that the nap operon structure of T. ammonificans is unique to this organism, and shares similarity with Desulfovibrio desulfuricans and other Deltaproteobacteria.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: All other Aquificae whose genomes are available have a Nap operon similar to that of Epsilon- and Gammaproteobacteria.
source: All other Aquificae whose genomes are available have a Nap operon similar to that of Epsilon- and Gammaproteobacteria (Vetriani et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis and citation to Vetriani et al., 2014

claim: The nitrate reductase of T. ammonificans appears to be of the monomeric type, and the NapB subunit is missing.
source: Moreover, unlike other members of the Aquificae, the nitrate reductase of T. ammonificans (encoded by gene Theam_0423, expressed in the proteome; Figure 3) appears to be of the monomeric type (sensu; Jepson et al., 2006), and the NapB subunit is missing (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on genome and proteome analysis with reference to Jepson et al., 2006 and Figure 3

claim: T. ammonificans is able to reduce elemental sulfur to hydrogen sulfide.
source: While T. ammonificans is able to reduce elemental sulfur to hydrogen sulfide (Vetriani et al., 2004), the sulfur reduction pathway remains unclear.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vetriani et al., 2004

claim: T. ammonificans is a strict anaerobe.
source: T. ammonificans is a strict anaerobe.
evidence: Based on established physiological characterization

claim: The genome of T. ammonificans codes for genes involved in the detoxification of oxygen radicals, including a catalase/peroxidase, a putative superoxide reductase, a cytochrome-C peroxidase and a cytochrome bd complex.
source: However, its genome codes for genes involved in the detoxification of oxygen radicals, including a catalase/peroxidase (Theam_0186), whose activity was previously detected (Vetriani et al., 2004), a putative superoxide reductase (Theam_0447), a cytochrome-C peroxidase (Theam_1156) and a cytochrome bd complex (Theam_0494–0496, Figure 3).
evidence: Based on genome analysis and citation to Vetriani et al., 2004, with reference to Figure 3

claim: The cytochrome bd complex has been shown to contribute to oxygen tolerance in other anaerobic bacteria.
source: The cythochrome bd complex has been shown to contribute to oxygen tolerance in other anaerobic bacteria (Das et al., 2005), and to contribute to the detoxification of nitrous oxide radicals (Mason et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Das et al., 2005 and Mason et al., 2009

claim: T. ammonificans possesses one to two terminal flagella.
source: T. ammonificans posses one to two terminal flagella (Vetriani et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vetriani et al., 2004

claim: When comparing the coding sequences (CDS) of T. ammonificans with available genomes, 34% of the CDS shared higher similarity to genes outside the Aquificae.
source: When comparing the coding sequences (CDS) of T. ammonificans with available genomes, 34% of the CDS shared higher similarity to genes outside the Aquificae, suggesting that these genes were acquired from more distantly related taxa.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: The simultaneous presence of two distinct carbon fixation pathways has been confirmed so far only in the endosymbiont of the deep-sea vent tubeworm Riftia pachyptila.
source: The simultaneous presence of two distinct carbon fixation pathways has been confirmed so far only in the endosymbiont of the deep-sea vent tubeworm Riftia pachyptila (Markert et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Markert et al., 2007

claim: The Riftia symbiont can switch from the Calvin-Benson-Bassham (CBB) to the rTCA cycles in response to low-energy supply.
source: Recent findings suggest that the Riftia symbiont can switch from the Calvin-Benson-Bassham (CBB) to the rTCA cycles in response to low-energy supply (e.g., low concentrations of hydrogen sulfide in the vent fluids, being the rTCA cycle more energetically favorable than the CBB cycle; Markert et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Markert et al., 2007

claim: Members of the Aquificaceae have the two-step version of the rTCA cycle, where citrate cleavage is accomplished by the combined action of the enzymes citryl-CoA synthetase and citryl-CoA lyase.
source: Members of the Aquificaceae (e.g., Aquifex aeolicus; Figure 9 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) have the two-step version of the rTCA cycle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), where citrate cleavage is accomplished by the combined action of the enzymes citryl-CoA synthetase and citryl-CoA lyase (encoded by the ccl gene), and the carboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate is catalyzed by the two enzymes 2-oxoglutarate carboxylase and oxalosuccinate reductase (Aoshima et al., 2004; Braakman and Smith, 2012).
evidence: Based on comparative analysis with citations to Aoshima et al., 2004 and Braakman and Smith, 2012, with reference to Figure 9 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The enzyme responsible for citrate cleavage, the ATP citrate lyase, likely evolved through gene fusion of the genes of CCS and CCL.
source: The enzyme responsible for citrate cleavage, the ATP citrate lyase, likely evolved through gene fusion of the genes of CCS and CCL (Aoshima et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aoshima et al., 2004

claim: Phylogenetic analyses of ACL suggests that the gene fusion event did not happen within the Aquificae, as Nitrospira and Chlorobia have an evolutionary older version of ACL than Hydrogenothermaceae and Desulfurobacteriaceae.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of ACL suggests that this gene fusion event did not happen within the Aquificae, as Nitrospira and Chlorobia have an evolutionary older version of ACL than Hydrogenothermaceae and Desulfurobacteriaceae (Figure 9; Hügler et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 9 and citation to Hügler et al., 2007

claim: It is likely that Hydrogenothermaceae and Desulfurobacteriaceae acquired ACL through horizontal gene transfer (HGT).
source: Hence, it is likely that these two groups acquired ACL through HGT (Figure 9 and Figure 8; Hügler et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis with citation to Hügler et al., 2007 and reference to Figures 8 and 9

claim: The two-step citrate cleavage is exclusive to the Aquificacea.
source: the two-step citrate cleavage is exclusive to the Aquificacea (Figure 9)
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 9

claim: The ccl gene is still present in the Hydrogenothermacea in addition to acl.
source: the ccl gene is still present in the Hydrogenothermacea (in addition to acl)
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: One sequenced strain of the Hydrogenothermaceae (S. azorense) still uses the two-step carboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate.
source: one sequenced strain of the Hydrogenothermaceae (S. azorense) still uses the two-step carboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate, suggesting that the two-step version of the rTCA cycle was present in the ancestor of both the Aquificaceae and the Hydrogenothermaceae (Figure 9 and Figure 10).
evidence: Based on genome analysis with reference to Figures 9 and 10

claim: Neither of the genes for the two-step citrate cleavage or two-step 2-oxoglutrate carboxylation is present in the Desulfurobacteriaceae.
source: However, neither of the genes for the two-step citrate cleavage or two-step 2-oxoglutrate carboxylation is present in the Desulfurobacteriaceae (Figure 9).
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 9

claim: The last common ancestor of the Aquificae had an incomplete form of the rTCA that did not proceed past the synthesis of 2-oxoglutarate.
source: Taking into consideration evidence from comparative genomics and phylogenetic analyses, the most parsimonious interpretation of the data suggests that the last common ancestor of the Aquificae had an incomplete form of the rTCA that did not proceed past the synthesis of 2-oxoglutarate
evidence: Inferred from comparative genomics and phylogenetic analyses

claim: The last common ancestor of the Aquificae possessed the complete reductive acetyl-CoA pathway.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that the last common ancestor of the Aquificae possessed the complete reductive acetyl-CoA pathway (Figure 10).
evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis and shown in Figure 10

claim: Members of the Desulfurobacteriaceae kept the CodH due to their obligate anaerobic lifestyle, while microaerophilic Aquificae (Hydrogenothermaceae and Aquificaceae) lost this extremely oxygen-sensitive enzyme.
source: While members of the Desulfurobacteriaceae kept the CodH due to their obligate anaerobic lifestyle, microaerophilic Aquificae (Hydrogenothermaceae and Aquificaceae) lost this extremely oxygen-sensitive enzyme (Figures 4 and 10).
evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis and shown in Figures 4 and 10

claim: The ancestor of Thermovibrio ammonificans was originally a hydrogen oxidizing, sulfur reducing bacterium that used a hybrid pathway for CO2 fixation.
source: We propose that the ancestor of the Aquificae was originally a hydrogen oxidizing, sulfur reducing bacterium that used a hybrid pathway for CO2 fixation.
evidence: Proposed based on integrated phylogenetic, comparative genomic and phylometabolic analyses

claim: With the gradual rise of oxygen in the atmosphere, more efficient terminal electron acceptors became available and the Aquificae lineage acquired genes that increased its metabolic flexibility while retaining ancestral metabolic traits.
source: With the gradual rise of oxygen in the atmosphere, more efficient terminal electron acceptors became available and this lineage acquired genes that increased its metabolic flexibility while retaining ancestral metabolic traits.
evidence: Proposed based on comparative genomic analysis and evolutionary inference

claim: The simultaneous presence of the rTCA cycle and of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway of carbon fixation in T. ammonificans may represent a modern analog of the early carbon fixation phenotype.
source: The simultaneous presence of the rTCA cycle and of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway of carbon fixation in T. ammonificans may represent a modern analog of the early carbon fixation phenotype, and suggests that the redundancy of central metabolic pathways was common in ancestral microorganisms.
evidence: Proposed based on metabolic reconstruction and evolutionary inference

claim: The redundancy of central metabolic pathways could have been common in ancestral microorganisms.
source: The simultaneous presence of the rTCA cycle and of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway of carbon fixation in T. ammonificans may represent a modern analog of the early carbon fixation phenotype, and suggests that the redundancy of central metabolic pathways was common in ancestral microorganisms.
evidence: Proposed based on metabolic reconstruction and evolutionary inference

claim: A recent reconstruction of the ancestral genome of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) suggests that LUCA was a hydrogen-dependent autotroph capable of S utilization that could fix CO2 via the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway.
source: Our findings are consistent with a recent reconstruction of the ancestral genome of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA), which suggest that LUCA was a hydrogen-dependent autotroph capable of S utilization that could fix CO2 via the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway (Weiss et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2016

claim: Part of the central metabolism of T. ammonificans is ancestral and emerged prior to oxygenic photosynthesis.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that part of the central metabolism of T. ammonificans is ancestral and emerged prior to oxygenic photosynthesis.
evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis and metabolic reconstruction

claim: The monomeric napA gene of T. ammonificans is homologous to that of Desulfovibrio desulfuricans and other Deltaproteobacteria and apparently has been acquired laterally.
source: The monomeric napA gene of T. ammonificans is homologous to that of Desulfovibrio desulfuricans and other Deltaproteobacteria (Figure 6; online interactive version) and apparently has been acquired laterally.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: The napA gene of T. ammonificans shares high similarity with assimilatory nitrate reductases (Nas) and could be an evolutionary intermediate form between assimilatory Nas and the dimeric respiratory Nap.
source: Furthermore, it shares high similarity with assimilatory nitrate reductases (Nas) and it could be an evolutionary intermediate form between assimilatory Nas and the dimeric respiratory Nap.
evidence: Inferred from sequence similarity analysis

claim: Group 1 Hyn hydrogenases are linked through the membrane quinone pool to nitrate reduction in T. ammonificans.
source: Based on the finding that Group 1 Hyn hydrogenases were expressed when T. ammonificans was grown under nitrate-reducing conditions (Figure 3), we suggest that these enzymes are linked through the membrane quinone pool to nitrate reduction and may have been acquired simultaneously with the nap genes.
evidence: Inferred from proteomic data shown in Figure 3

claim: Oxygen-stress related genes in T. ammonificans are not part of the core, or ancestral genome, but evolved as a response to exposure to toxic oxygen radicals.
source: We propose that such genes are not part of the core, or ancestral genome of T. ammonificans, but that they evolved as a response to exposure to toxic oxygen radicals.
evidence: Proposed based on comparative genomic analysis and evolutionary inference

claim: The nitrate reduction pathway and oxygen stress-related genes may represent adaptations acquired by the T. ammonificans lineage to cope with the rise of oxygen on Earth.
source: In conclusion, the nitrate reduction pathway, as well as oxygen stress-related genes, may represent adaptations acquired by the T. ammonificans lineage to cope with the rise of oxygen on Earth.
evidence: Proposed based on comparative genomic analysis and evolutionary inference

claim: The reductive acetyl-CoA pathway is present in acetogenic bacteria, methanogens, sulfate-reducers and anammox bacteria.
source: The key enzyme of this carbon fixation pathway, which is found in acetogens, methanogens, sulfate-reducers and anaerobic ammonium oxidizers (anammox; Berg et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Berg et al., 2010

claim: The key enzyme of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway is the bifunctional heterotetramer enzyme carbon monoxide dehydrogenase/acetyl-CoA synthase (CODH/ACS).
source: The key enzyme of this carbon fixation pathway, which is found in acetogens, methanogens, sulfate-reducers and anaerobic ammonium oxidizers (anammox; Berg et al., 2010), is the bifunctional heterotetramer enzyme carbon monoxide dehydrogenase/acetyl-CoA synthase (CODH/ACS).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berg et al., 2010 and established knowledge

claim: Sequence analysis of the T. ammonificans CodH protein sequence revealed the presence of conserved residues necessary for the interaction with Acs and for the coordination of the NiFeS cluster.
source: Sequence analysis of the T. ammonificans CodH protein sequence revealed the presence of conserved residues necessary for the interaction with Acs and for the coordination of the NiFeS cluster.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis

claim: The type V CodH may catalyze the reduction of CO2 to CO.
source: We hypothesize that the type V CodH, which, based on structural and size considerations may represent the most ancestral version of this class of enzymes (Frank Robb, personal communication), may catalyze the reduction of CO2 to CO.
evidence: Proposed based on structural considerations and inference

claim: Within the Aquificae, the type V CodH is exclusive to the Desulfurobacteriaceae.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that, within the Aquificae, the type V CodH is exclusive to the Desulfurobacteriaceae.
evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis

claim: The reductive acetyl-CoA pathway could be operational in T. ammonificans in addition to the rTCA cycle.
source: The retrieval of the CodH enzyme from the proteome of T. ammonificans (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1), along with the catalytic subunit of the formate dehydrogenase (FdhA), suggests that the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway could be operational in T. ammonificans in addition to the rTCA cycle.
evidence: Inferred from proteomic data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1

claim: The use of different carbon fixation strategies could be advantageous under energy limiting conditions, could optimize overall carbon fixation or provide different precursors for biosynthetic pathways.
source: The use of different carbon fixation strategies could be advantageous under energy limiting conditions (e.g., deep biosphere), could optimize overall carbon fixation or provide different precursors for biosynthetic pathways, and could be more widespread than originally thought.
evidence: Proposed based on inference from metabolic analysis

claim: The presence of a reductive acetyl-CoA pathway in T. ammonificans and other members of the Desulfurobacteriaceae supports the scenario that a complete and operational reductive acetyl-CoA pathway was present in the ancestor of the phylum Aquificae.
source: Furthermore, this finding supports the scenario proposed by Braakman and Smith that a complete and operational reductive acetyl-CoA pathway was present in the ancestor of the phylum Aquificae (Braakman and Smith, 2012).
evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis and supported by citation to Braakman and Smith, 2012

claim: The rise of oxygen has been interpreted as one of the factors responsible for the diversification of carbon fixation from the ancestral pathway.
source: The rise of oxygen has been interpreted as one of the factors responsible for the diversification of carbon fixation from the ancestral pathway, and could explain the subsequent loss of the CodH in the generally facultative microaerobic Hydrogenothermaceae and Aquificaceae within the Aquificae (Table 2).
evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis with reference to Table 2

claim: A complete rTCA cycle could have evolved in the Aquificaceae from an ancestral, incomplete version of the cycle.
source: Since citryl-CoA synthetase and 2-oxoglutarate carboxylase likely evolved by duplication of the genes for the succinyl-CoA synthetase and pyruvate carboxylase (Aoshima, 2007; Braakman and Smith, 2012), a complete rTCA cycle could have evolved in the Aquificaceae from an ancestral, incomplete version of the cycle.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary analysis with citations to Aoshima, 2007 and Braakman and Smith, 2012

claim: Temperature may have played a role in preserving the ancient, more symmetric, two-step citrate cleavage rTCA cycle variant in Aquificaceae.
source: We hypothesize that temperature may also have played a role in preserving the ancient, more symmetric, two-step citrate cleavage rTCA cycle variant in Aquificaceae (Figure 10).
evidence: Proposed based on inference from comparative analysis shown in Figure 10

claim: Members of Aquificaceae have optimum growth temperatures (75–95°C) higher than those of the two other groups (60–75°C).
source: Members of this group have optimum growth temperatures (75–95°C) higher than those of the two other groups (60–75°C; Table 1), and the 'ancient' enzymes might be more stable at these high temperatures.
evidence: Based on data from Table 1

claim: The 'newer' enzymes that catalyze the one-step citrate cleavage might have evolved to function optimally at lower temperatures.
source: In contrast, the 'newer' enzymes that catalyze the one-step citrate cleavage might have evolved to function optimally at lower temperatures.
evidence: Proposed based on inference from temperature and enzyme evolution

claim: All the extant members of the Aquificae phylum possess the genes encoding for the enzymes of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway, with the exception of codH (encoding for the CO-dehydrogenase), which is only found in the Desulfurobacteriaceae.
source: Different members of the Aquificae use either one of the two versions of the rTCA cycle, and all the extant members of this phylum possess the genes encoding for the enzymes of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway, with the exception of codH (encoding for the CO-dehydrogenase), which is only found in the Desulfurobacteriaceae.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: The last common ancestor of the Aquificae combined the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway with an incomplete form of the rTCA that did not proceed past the synthesis of 2-oxoglutarate.
source: Alltogether, our results suggest that the last common ancestor of the Aquificae combined the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway with an incomplete form of the rTCA that did not proceed past the synthesis of 2-oxoglutarate (Figure 10).
evidence: Inferred from integrated phylogenetic and comparative genomic analyses shown in Figure 10

claim: An incomplete version of the rTCA pathway, consisting only of the reactions from acetyl-CoA to 2-oxoglutarate, is present in extant methanogens.
source: A similar incomplete version of the rTCA pathway, consisting only of the reactions from acetyl-CoA to 2-oxoglutarate, is present in extant methanogens (Berg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berg, 2011

claim: The phylometabolic reconstruction of the ancestral state of carbon fixation in the Aquificae is conceptually consistent with chemoautotrophic processes of extant Bacteria and Archaea, and may represent the earliest carbon fixation pathway.
source: Thus, our phylometabolic reconstruction of the ancestral state of carbon fixation in the Aquificae (Figure 10) is conceptually consistent with chemoautotrophic processes of extant Bacteria and Archaea, and may represent the earliest carbon fixation pathway.
evidence: Proposed based on phylometabolic reconstruction shown in Figure 10
